title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
summary: "Do not ask again" prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.
article:
If you’ve ever breezed past a popup asking for permission without pausing to read the fine print, there’s a good chance your sensitive data is currently waving hello from a public GitHub repository. Anthropic’s AI coding assistant, Claude Code, is at the center of a surprising security slip-up where a seemingly harmless “Do not ask again” checkbox is accidentally spilling passwords, API keys, and other secrets across the internet.

Here’s what happened: Claude Code occasionally asks users for permission to access project files, environment variables, or integrated services. For the sake of a smooth workflow, the tool offers a “Do not ask again” option. But as it turns out, checking that box was saving user authorizations–along with the credentials tied to them–and in some cases, those authorization tokens were being packed into configuration files that got pushed to Git repositories. The result? Secrets that were meant to stay on a developer’s machine are now publicly indexable on GitHub.

Why does this matter? Because AI coding tools are becoming central to how software gets built, and they often need access to the very things that keep applications running–database passwords, cloud API tokens, third-party service keys. When those get accidentally committed to a repo, they don’t just sit there; they get scanned, harvested, and potentially misused by anyone with a cursor and a search engine. It’s not a hack of Anthropic’s servers, but it is a stark reminder that the easiest way to leak a secret is often through a click designed to save us time.

The interesting part? This isn’t a flaw in the AI’s reasoning–it’s a UI/UX design choice that prioritized workflow continuity over a safety net. A prompt that says “Do not ask again” should probably come with a side of “and here’s exactly what you’re agreeing to persist.”

For now, developers using Claude Code are being urged to double-check their .gitignore files, audit recent commits for stray credentials, and maybe think twice before that checkbox earns a permanent spot in their muscle memory. Anthropic is reportedly looking into the behavior, but the incident serves as a timely caution: in the race to let AI write code, we shouldn’t let it write our security risks too.

title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
summary: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings native 15-second video generation and editing, stronger consistency, and 30% lower pricing.
article:
Move over, static images—there’s a new mover and shaker in town. Google just dropped Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and it’s bringing native 15-second video generation to the masses without the usual hefty compute bill. Announced as the latest fast-and-friendly addition to the Gemini family, this model packs longer clips, tighter consistency, and a pricing slash that’s roughly 30% lighter on the wallet. For developers and AI tinkerers who’ve been itching to add motion to their projects without budgeting for a small data center, this is the kind of upgrade that feels less like a chore and more like a playground opening up. Let’s break down what’s actually new, why it matters, and why you might want to pay attention.

First up: the star feature. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash now supports native 15-second video generation and editing. Earlier attempts at AI video often felt like watching a GIF that forgot how to loop—choppy, inconsistent, or stuck in a three-second loop. Gemini’s new native approach means the model understands timing, transitions, and visual continuity from start to finish. The result? Fewer “wait, did the object just teleport?” moments and more coherent scenes that actually feel like a clip, not a glitch reel.

Then there’s consistency. Google says the model sports “stronger consistency,” which in plain speak means your characters, objects, and styles stay put across frames. No more wonky anatomy or lighting that changes shot by shot. For devs building storytelling tools, avatars, or interactive ads, this is the difference between a demo that wows and one that becomes a meme for the wrong reasons. It also means less time spent fixing AI hallucinations in post, and more time shipping features.

Pricing is where the “Flash” part really earns its keep. At 30% lower cost compared to its predecessor, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash makes high-quality video generation accessible to indie developers, bootstrapped startups, and hobbyists who previously might have felt priced out of the video AI game. Lower latency and lower cost don’t just mean savings—they mean faster iteration. You can test, tweak, and deploy ideas in hours instead of days, which is the kind of agility that turns prototypes into products.

Whether you’re a dev itching to plug video generation into your next app, an AI enthusiast curious about what 15-second natively generated clips look like, or just someone who enjoys watching tech get faster and cheaper, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is worth a look. It’s not trying to replace Hollywood, but it’s certainly lowering the bar for what’s possible on a developer’s laptop and budget. Keep an eye on the release notes, fire up your API keys, and get ready to make your apps move—without making your wallet sweat.

title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
summary: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components.  The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in […]
article:
**Robots Graduating from the Gym to the Workshop**

If your robot vacuum could suddenly learn to thread a needle, you’d probably call it magic. But at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), the trick isn’t sorcery—it’s smarter simulation. NVIDIA and a crew of partners just showed how the same virtual playgrounds that taught bots to walk, roll, and hop are now being put to work on much finer stuff: aligning gears, connecting cables, and assembling tiny components without breaking a sweat.

For years, simulation has been the go-to proving ground for locomotion. It’s easy to render a thousand iterations of a robot stumbling, recovering, and eventually finding its balance. But move the goalposts to manipulation—think precise hand-eye coordination, delicate forces, and sub-millimeter tolerances—and the challenge spikes. The NVIDIA team and their collaborators revealed a pivot: using highly detailed, physics-accurate simulation to let robots “rehearse” these tricky tasks in virtual space before they ever touch real hardware. The result? Faster learning, fewer broken parts, and robots that can actually perform the kind of delicate work that underpins everything from electronics manufacturing to home assistance.

Why does this matter? Because for all the hype about autonomous cars and warehouse bots, the real frontier for useful robotics lies in dexterity. A robot that can navigate a messy kitchen is impressive; one that can swap a tiny capacitor onto a circuit board or snap a connector into place without snapping the part itself? That’s transformative. By shifting the heavy lifting of skill acquisition into simulation, researchers can test thousands of variations in seconds, identify the subtlest successful strategies, and transfer those refined behaviors into the real world with minimal trial-and-error.

The takeaway from CoRL is clear: the era of robots learning to move is giving way to an era of robots learning to do. And with NVIDIA and its partners leading the charge, the next time you watch a bot fumble a screw, it might just be because it’s still practicing its touch—in the safest, most effective classroom there is.
